Empirical Research Plan  
“Group Performance Incentives for Teachers and Pupil Achievement in Israel”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
-------------------------------------------------
Preferred design: Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with an event-study.

Rationale  
• Policy is introduced to a subset of schools while others remain untreated → clear treated vs. control units.  
• We observe multiple pre- and post-treatment years at the student level → allows school and year fixed effects and testing of pre-trends.  
• Treatment is discrete and starts at a known date; no obviously sharp running variable → RDD not applicable.  
• No credible external instrument beyond the policy rollout itself.  

The event-study extension lets us (i) visualise and test the parallel-trends assumption and (ii) study dynamics and persistence of effects.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
-------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  TREAT_s = 1 if school s participates in the group-performance incentive programme in year t or thereafter; 0 otherwise.  
  POST_t = 1 for years ≥ first year of implementation; 0 otherwise.  
  The interaction TREAT_s × POST_t is the main DID regressor.

Control group  
  Comparable elementary schools that never (or not yet) adopt the programme during the sample horizon.

Treatment timing  
  Policy year = 0 (e.g. 2001) in participating schools; other schools keep POST=0 throughout.  
  If some schools join later waves, we will employ a staggered‐adoption DID with the “Sun & Abraham (2021)” estimator to avoid negative weighting problems.

Unit of analysis  
  Student i in school s, grade g, year t.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In absence of the programme, pupil achievement in treated and control schools would have followed the same trajectory.  
  Plausibility: Schools were reportedly selected based on administrative capacity rather than test-score growth; we will test it via event-study leads.

A2. No simultaneous confounding reforms that differentially hit treated schools exactly at implementation.  
  Plausibility: Israeli MoE did not launch other large reforms in exactly those schools/years; we will investigate policy records and add year-by-district × poverty fixed effects.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): A school’s treatment does not affect outcomes in control schools.  
  Plausibility: Students seldom transfer across catchment areas; teacher interaction across schools limited. We will test by dropping neighbouring schools.

A4. Composition stability: Treatment does not induce selective entry/exit of students or teachers that itself drives scores.  
  Plausibility: Some teacher reshuffling may occur; we will control for observable student and teacher composition and test robustness to balanced panels.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
-------------------------------------------------
T1. Non-random programme assignment (selection on growth trends).  
 Mitigation:  
  • Pre-period event-study coefficients (–3 to –1) must be individually and jointly ≈0.  
  • Propensity-score or entropy balancing re-weighting to equalise observables.  
  • School × linear-time trends as robustness.

T2. Student or teacher sorting after announcement (composition bias).  
 Mitigation:  
  • Track cohort-level prior achievement; include lagged average scores as controls.  
  • Estimate effects on movers separately; show results for balanced sample.

T3. Spillovers / general-equilibrium effects (e.g., control-school teachers discouraged).  
 Mitigation:  
  • Spatial exclusion: drop control schools within 10 km of treated schools.  
  • Placebo: use high-school data (not targeted by policy) as falsification.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast fixed-effects regressions
library(ggplot2)
library(did)           # Sun & Abraham estimator
# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load & merge data
# -------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("israeli_school_panel.csv")   # one row per student-year

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# -------------------------------------------------
# indicator for treatment school (time-invariant)
dt[, treat := as.integer(school_treated == 1)]

# first year of treatment per school
dt[, first_treat_year := min(year[treat == 1]), by = school_id]

# post indicator (staggered adoption: 1 if year >= first treat year)
dt[, post := as.integer(year >= first_treat_year)]
dt[is.na(post), post := 0]  # control schools

# interaction
dt[, did := treat * post]

# relative year for event study
dt[, rel_year := ifelse(treat == 1, year - first_treat_year, -999)]
dt[, rel_year_factor := factor(rel_year)]

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID specification
# -------------------------------------------------
fe_formula <- score ~ did + student_gender + student_SES | school_id + year
did_mod <- feols(fe_formula, data = dt, cluster = ~school_id)
summary(did_mod)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study with Sun & Abraham
# -------------------------------------------------
sa_mod <- att_gt(yname = "score",
                 tname = "year",
                 idname = "school_id",
                 gname = "first_treat_year",
                 xformla = ~ student_gender + student_SES,
                 data = dt,
                 clustervars = "school_id")

es <- aggte(sa_mod, type = "dynamic")
summary(es)

# Plot event-study
plot_df <- data.frame(rel_year = es$egt, att = es$att, se = es$se)
ggplot(plot_df[plot_df$rel_year >= -3 & plot_df$rel_year <= 5, ],
       aes(rel_year, att)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = att - 1.96*se, ymax = att + 1.96*se), width = .2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Years relative to treatment", y = "ATT on test scores")

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: propensity-score reweighting
# -------------------------------------------------
# quick P-score via logit
ps_mod <- glm(treat ~ pre_score + avg_SES + school_size + urban,
              data = dt[year == min(year)], family = binomial)
dt[, ps := predict(ps_mod, type = "response")]
dt[, w := treat/ps + (1-treat)/(1-ps)]   # IPTW

did_ps <- feols(score ~ did | school_id + year,
                data = dt, weights = ~w, cluster = ~school_id)
summary(did_ps)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
-------------------------------------------------
Direction: Positive—group bonuses should incentivise teachers to co-operate and raise average achievement.  
Magnitude (prior): 0.05–0.10 σ increase in test scores in the first year, potentially rising to 0.15 σ after 3 years if collaboration effects compound. Economic theory (team incentives with peer monitoring) predicts moderate but nontrivial gains.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Difference-in-Differences)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable/absent)  
C1 Parallel pre-trends visually flat and statistically indistinguishable …… 1  
C2 No coinciding policies/exogenous shocks in treated vs. control schools … 0  
C3 No spillovers or SUTVA violations …………………………………………………………… 0  
C4 Stable composition of students and teachers ……………………………………… 0  
C5 Common support for observables & treatment probability ……………… 1  

Overall, we are confident in C1 and C5; C2-C4 require careful robustness checks outlined above.
